title: Cornell campus Flock control baseline
summary: Request #1900 advances the Cornell campus Flock investigation by separating the reported seven-camera deployment from Cornell's current Policy 8.1 centralized-surveillance control requirements and Faculty Senate governance record.

data.question: What Cornell-wide governance and access-control requirements can be established around the reported seven-camera Flock deployment?
data.method: Reconciled the existing Cornell Flock targets with current Cornell Policy 8.1, the Access Control Program's first-party role description, Faculty Senate Resolution 198, and March 2026 independent reporting on the seven-camera deployment.
data.framework: University-wide policy authority and required centralized camera visibility are distinct from proof of Flock-platform integration, credentials, actual access, sharing, or query activity.
data.scope: Public institutional governance and reported campus Flock deployment; no private-person enrichment.
findings: Independent reporting identifies seven Flock cameras operating at major entry points to central Cornell campus since October 2024.

Current Cornell Policy 8.1 requires security cameras to be integrated into the centralized security video surveillance system unless exempted and says cameras must be viewable by the Division of Public Safety Communications Center, Cornell University Police Department, and Access Control Program.
Cornell's Access Control Program describes itself as providing centralized video-surveillance services and Policy 8.1 compliance tooling.

Faculty Senate Resolution 198 passed December 20, 2024 and demanded public information and governance consultation concerning increased police/security presence and security cameras; the official archive records an administration response dated February 10, 2025.
conclusions: Cornell has an authoritative centralized surveillance-control framework applicable to campus security cameras generally.
The public evidence reviewed does not establish whether the seven Flock cameras were integrated into that centralized system or which units held Flock-platform credentials.
No directed Ithaca Police to Cornell Police sharing edge is established by these policy materials.
recommendations: Recover the native Flock contract, procurement, invoices, renewal, data-processing, support, and termination terms.
Recover the serial-level seven-camera inventory and exact Flock platform users, roles, administrators, audit exports, sharing configuration, and retention/deletion evidence.
Recover the February 10, 2025 administration response and subsequent implementation records tied to Resolution 198.
counterarguments: Policy 8.1 may apply through an integration layer rather than direct Flock credentials, so required visibility cannot be translated into platform-user identities without evidence.
The seven-camera count and start date are independently reported rather than established here through a native inventory.
limitations: No native Flock contract or platform export was recovered.
No serial-level camera inventory or verified 30-day lifecycle sample was recovered.
unresolved: Were the seven Flock cameras integrated into Cornell's centralized security video system?
Which Cornell units and named roles actually held Flock access?
What retention, sharing, audit, and deletion settings were configured?
Did any directed CUPD-IPD access edge exist?

classification_rules: Reuse stable canonical IDs when materially equivalent targets already exist.
University policy requirements do not prove direct Flock-platform credentials or actual access.
Institutional camera visibility and Flock directed sharing are separate predicates.
Cornell and Ithaca municipal networks remain separate absent a documented directed access edge.

findings.finding: Six existing canonical Cornell targets cover contract, inventory, sharing, audits, deletion, and centralized access and were reused.
Cornell Policy 8.1 establishes a centralized camera-visibility requirement for DPS Communications, CUPD, and Access Control Program unless an exemption applies.
The official Faculty Senate archive documents Resolution 198's passage and later administration response, establishing a governance trail for increased campus camera deployment.
Actual Flock platform integration, users, sharing, audit records, and retention remain unresolved.
